claim: A scoring rule is strictly proper if and only if reporting one's true probability distribution uniquely maximises expected score, making honest reporting the dominant strategy.
title: Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation

claim: For categorical outcomes the Brier, logarithmic and spherical rules are proper; the multi-class Brier score is bounded while the logarithmic score is unbounded on a confident miss.
title: Proper scoring rules for estimation and forecast evaluation

claim: Point forecasts are only meaningfully scorable against an elicitable functional; zero-one loss on a categorical label is consistent for the mode and does not elicit strength of belief.
title: Making and Evaluating Point Forecasts

claim: About one hour of probabilistic-reasoning training improved forecasters' Brier scores by roughly 6 to 11 percent over controls, replicated across four tournament years.
title: Developing expert political judgment: The impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments

claim: Across thousands of forecasters and hundreds of events under scored feedback, confidence tracked accuracy closely and systematic overconfidence did not dominate.
title: Confidence Calibration in a Multiyear Geopolitical Forecasting Competition
authors: Moore, Swift, Minster, Mellers, Ungar, Tetlock, Yang, Tenney

claim: When forecasters care about relative standing rather than their own score, the optimal report is more extreme than their true belief, so competition breaks propriety.
title: Probability Elicitation, Scoring Rules, and Competition Among Forecasters

claim: Awarding a prize to the single best total score is not incentive compatible because extreme reports raise the probability of winning; a randomised prize mechanism restores truthful reporting.
title: Incentive-Compatible Forecasting Competitions
authors: Witkowski, Freeman, Wortman Vaughan, Pennock, Krause

claim: In prediction tournaments over on the order of a hundred questions the winner is frequently not the best forecaster because noise dominates.
title: A Prediction Tournament Paradox

claim: Foldit players outperformed automated structure refinement on problems requiring large backbone rearrangements, with competition and collaboration driving exploration of search strategies.
title: Predicting protein structures with a multiplayer online game
authors: Cooper, Khatib, Treuille, Barbero, Lee, Beenen, Leaver-Fay, Baker, Popovic

claim: EteRNA's retention and scientific value came from a wet-lab feedback loop in which player designs were synthesised and the measured result returned, yielding design rules automated methods missed.
title: RNA design rules from a massive open laboratory
authors: Lee, Kladwang, Lee, Cantu, Azizyan, Kim, Limpaecher, Yoon, Treuille, Das

claim: In Phylo the genetics was hidden behind coloured blocks; puzzles with more distinct player solutions improved alignments more often, and only solutions beating a par baseline were admitted.
title: Phylo: A Citizen Science Approach for Improving Multiple Sequence Alignment
authors: Kawrykow, Roumanis, Kam, Kwak, Leung, Wu, Zarour, Sarmenta, Blanchette, Waldispuhl

claim: Eyewire gated players on an accuracy threshold against previously reconstructed data and routed every reconstruction through independent players plus expert review.
title: Space-time wiring specificity supports direction selectivity in the retina
authors: Kim, Greene, Zlateski, Lee, Richardson, Turaga, Purcaro, Balkam, Robinson, Behabadi, Campos, Denk, Seung

claim: The claim that Quantum Moves players beat optimisation algorithms failed because the algorithmic baseline was weak; standard optimisation beat every player solution.
title: Algorithms Clearly Beat Gamers at Quantum Moves. A Verification

claim: Merely showing people others' estimates collapsed the diversity of estimates without improving accuracy and raised confidence in the wrong answer.
title: How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect

claim: Ranking motivated Foldit play but led top players to hoard technique, while un-gamified Galaxy Zoo volunteers rejected rankings as anti-scientific.
title: Getting it Right or Being Top Rank: Games in Citizen Science

claim: A points-and-leaderboard game that only re-judged existing citizen-science submissions improved them, with experts siding with the game in most disagreements and about fifteen votes sufficing.
title: The CrowdWater game: A playful way to improve the accuracy of crowdsourced water level class data

claim: Citizen-science data quality is protected by training and testing volunteers, expert validation, replication across volunteers, and statistical error modelling.
title: Assessing data quality in citizen science

claim: Generating a rhythm-game chart from a stream decomposes into step placement (when) and step selection (which), with placement conditioned on a difficulty label.
title: Dance Dance Convolution

claim: Prior rhythm-chart generators failed on patterning, the congruent relation between placed objects, which human raters treat as the marker of a good chart.
title: TaikoNation: Patterning-focused Chart Generation for Rhythm Action Games

claim: Procedural content generation is most effective when generation is steered by a model of player experience rather than by fidelity to source data.
title: Experience-Driven Procedural Content Generation

claim: Spectator enjoyment of StarCraft comes from types of information asymmetry that create suspense; an omniscient view kills tension.
title: Starcraft from the stands: understanding the game spectator

claim: Badges on Stack Overflow shifted the mixture of user actions toward the rewarded action, with effort accelerating near a badge boundary.
title: Steering user behavior with badges

claim: A meta-analysis of gamification in learning found small effects, with only the cognitive effect stable under high-rigor studies.
title: The Gamification of Learning: a Meta-analysis

claim: A sixteen-week course with leaderboards and badges produced lower intrinsic motivation, satisfaction and final exam scores than the identical ungamified course.
title: Assessing the effects of gamification in the classroom: A longitudinal study on intrinsic motivation, social comparison, satisfaction, effort, and academic performance

claim: Points, levels and leaderboards increased output quantity but did not raise competence satisfaction or intrinsic motivation, acting as extrinsic incentives rather than informational feedback.
title: Towards understanding the effects of individual gamification elements on intrinsic motivation and performance

claim: In software engineering education, loss of performance was the most frequently reported negative effect of gamification and the leaderboard the most cited element behind negative effects.
title: Negative effects of gamification in education software: Systematic mapping and practitioner perceptions

claim: Task-involving comments raised interest and performance while numerical grades, even alongside comments, undermined both.
title: Enhancing and undermining intrinsic motivation: The effects of task-involving and ego-involving evaluation on interest and performance

claim: Across 607 effect sizes feedback helped on average but over a third of interventions decreased performance, with effectiveness falling as attention moved toward the self and away from the task.
title: The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory

claim: Measuring an activity increased how much people did it but reduced enjoyment, because attention to output made the activity feel like work, with no external reward attached.
title: The Hidden Cost of Personal Quantification

claim: Seven types of engaging uncertainty arise from three sources, game, player and outcome, tied chiefly to curiosity and competence motives.
title: The Role of Uncertainty in Moment-to-Moment Player Motivation: A Grounded Theory

claim: Errors made with high confidence are corrected better than low-confidence errors because surprise draws attention to the feedback.
title: Surprising feedback improves later memory

claim: A Markov decision process director can assemble levels from a fixed pool of pre-authored segments to match measured player skill.
title: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment via Procedural Level Generation Guided by a Markov Decision Process for Platformers

claim: Legibility, the observer inferring the goal quickly, and predictability, motion matching expectation given a known goal, are formally distinct and often contradictory.
title: Legibility and predictability of robot motion

claim: A literature review of empirical gamification studies found that reported effects depend on the context and on the users.
title: Does Gamification Work? A Literature Review of Empirical Studies on Gamification
